title: Tax-free minimum wage, mortgage costs and election pledges
summary:
Spain's government promises another tax-free minimum wage rise as new mortgages become more expensive. We cover pension and Senate election stakes, transport and education strikes, and Spanish football's awards haul.

Enjoying Spain Daily? Support us: https://buymeacoffee.com/spanified

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Did Spanish football leave any trophies for anyone else?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Eight of twelve awards in London. And Alexia Putellas won her third Ballon d'Or. wow

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Eight of twelve! So who still went home without the biggest prize?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Keep that question. We'll come back to it after the news.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Good morning! It's Tuesday, the twenty-seventh of October, and this is Spain Daily, from Spanified dot com!

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: I'm Inna, here with Dima. Today: dearer mortgages, and why Madrid suddenly lost some wealthy taxpayers.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: First, the government's promise to keep the next minimum wage rise free of income tax.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Veinte Minutos reports that the government plans another minimum wage rise free of personal income tax. Government spokesperson Elma Saiz confirmed the commitment yesterday. About two and a half million workers earn the minimum wage.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: The Labour Ministry's advisers are designing an increase to protect purchasing power. That implies a rise of at least around three point six percent. The ministry plans to publish its proposal during the week of November second. Ministers will then set the amount.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Oh, the tax part matters. Workers shouldn't lose part of that increase to income tax. right More reaching their bank accounts.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: But Inna, it's an election-season promise with the amount still missing. When do we actually get a figure?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: The proposal comes first, then the Council of Ministers approves the amount, probably before the November twenty-ninth elections.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Does the tax protection move with whatever amount ministers approve, rather than staying at the old wage?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: The government says it'll update the tax deduction to match. exactly That's the part protecting take-home pay.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Borrowing costs are moving upward too. Veinte Minutos reports Spain's average new-mortgage rate passed three percent in August. The average loan reached a record of roughly a hundred and eighty-one thousand euros. Banks tightened lending requirements as Euribor, the benchmark used by many variable mortgages, rose. Mortgage signings nevertheless increased.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Huh. Rates up, lending tighter, and yet people still sign?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Spain also slipped from third to fifth-cheapest in the eurozone, so it's less of a bargain than before.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Mm. And Euribor has risen four months in a row, so the pressure comes from both sides.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Europa Press reports Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez pledged constitutional protection for pension rises linked to consumer prices yesterday. Speaking at a rally in Gijón, he promised the reform if he remains in government after November twenty-ninth. It is an election pledge, not a formal proposal. An ordinary reform needs two hundred and ten deputies, while a majority in Congress is a hundred and seventy-six.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Constitutional power is also at stake in the Senate, Spain's upper house. El Mundo's projection says a PP-Vox candidacy pact could, in the best case, reach the hundred and sixty-one seats needed to appoint four Constitutional Court magistrates without the Socialists, ending the court's progressive majority.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Hold on. Could Sánchez pass his pension protection with just enough seats to govern?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: He'd need far more than a plain majority. And the Senate figure is only the projection's best case.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: The pension promise speaks straight to retirement income. true The Senate ballot could shape who rules on laws affecting everyone.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Right, and both get decided on November twenty-ninth.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Veinte Minutos reports a hundred and thirty arrests, mostly minors, after Barcelona's October twenty-fourth protests ended in looting and fires. Anonymous TikTok accounts spread the call as a protest over secondary schools. Mayor Jaume Collboni estimated street furniture damage at about thirty-six thousand euros. He promised support for affected shops. An investigation is underway.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: In Bilbao yesterday, El Mundo reports nineteen arrests after street fires involving around three hundred youths. Most people had already left a protest against a cancelled appearance by influencer Vito Quiles. Those remaining burned vehicles and bins in Deusto, a city neighbourhood. A Local Police motorbike and several cars burned.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Who organised the Barcelona call?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Authorities haven't attributed it to a group. The government has asked people to await the investigation.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Catalan president Salvador Illa and Basque regional president Imanol Pradales both condemned the violence.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Dima, what does the Supreme Court want from the government over citizens affected by the Ley de Nietos?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: The court wants a list of everyone naturalised under that law, which gives citizenship to descendants of Spaniards. It is due around Wednesday, October twenty-eighth. Veinte Minutos reports a CEU-CEFAS study estimates about two hundred and fifty thousand voters were added to the overseas roll, eighty-seven thousand more than the government has identified. Their voting rights are suspended for the November twenty-ninth election.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Oof. So a person abroad with a Spanish passport from this route cannot vote on November twenty-ninth?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: For now, yes. The court wants the names of everyone naturalised this way.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Which is why the deadline matters. The list will show whose numbers are right.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Spanish football had a much brighter night in London. El Mundo reports Spain won eight of twelve Ballon d'Or awards. Alexia Putellas won her third women's Ballon d'Or. Lamine Yamal took his third youth prize, but missed the main men's award.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Spain coach Luis de la Fuente and Barcelona women's coach Pere Romeu also won. Unai Simón and Cata Coll took goalkeeper prizes. Vicky López won the women's youth award, and Barcelona won best women's team.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: There's our answer: Yamal missed the main men's award. Does that spoil the night?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: I'd give the women's success the spotlight. Players, coaches, goalkeepers, the team itself. oh nice That's quite a spread.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Fair. Even Rafael Louzán, the head of the Spanish football federation, called it a golden era.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: A different kind of money story. El País reports a study linking the state wealth tax to Madrid's first net outflow of wealthy taxpayers. The shift came in twenty twenty-three among people worth above three point seven million euros. Regions including Madrid stopped granting rebates, removing the financial incentive to move.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: The tax raised almost six hundred million euros annually in Madrid alone. But asset restructuring also reduced taxable wealth. Researcher Dmitry Petrov says it's too early to credit the tax alone for the movement between regions.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: So the incentive to move disappeared, but people still found ways to cut the bill?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: That's the tension. Less reason to change regions, but more reason to rearrange assets around exemptions. mhm

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: So the wealthy shifted from moving house to tax planning.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: La Vanguardia reports a nationwide Renfe drivers' strike on Thursday, October twenty-ninth, from just after midnight until late evening. In Catalonia, minimum services require sixty-six percent at peak times and thirty-three percent otherwise. The drivers' union wants stronger safety protocols during weather alerts, putting safety ahead of maintaining services.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: What should passengers do before setting off? This affects journeys across Spain, not just Catalonia.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Renfe advises planning ahead and checking service status before travelling. Frequencies may change.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Those Catalan minimums apply there. Check your own service rather than assuming your usual train will run.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Household finances remain under pressure. El País reports severe material and social deprivation affected about eight percent of people last year. Among households with children under sixteen, it was nearly eleven percent. Spain now has the EU's fifth-highest rate despite economic growth. Funcas calls for family support, including housing help and school meal assistance.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Economic growth hasn't reached every household. Does Funcas want help aimed specifically at families?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Cash support per child and affordable early education are among its proposals, alongside help with school materials.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Madrid's education dispute continues. El País reports the strike committee threatens court action unless the regional government negotiates. The strike began October fourteenth. Demands include six hundred euros more monthly, in fourteen payments, and smaller classes. Education councillor Mercedes Zarzalejo calls the demands unachievable and says talks on teaching careers are already open.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Why haven't those existing talks resolved the demand to negotiate?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Unions say the teaching-career discussions weren't among their demands. Families face a continuing dispute over staffing, pay and classroom conditions.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Finally, a year-end spending signal. Veinte Minutos reports a new survey of autónomos, Spain's self-employed workers, finds roughly fifty-eight percent plan price rises before year-end. Higher energy and production costs are squeezing businesses. Around one in six fears closure or major contraction within three years, a larger share than in June.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: For customers, another increase hurts. But can a small business keep absorbing higher costs indefinitely?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Many say they can't. And most already raised prices in the past year.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Coming up: the court's list deadline around October twenty-eighth, Thursday's rail strike, then the wage proposal week of November second.
